newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: European security summit opens in Lisbon.
newsitem.headline: European security summit opens in Lisbon.

text.p: Leaders from Europe and North America opened a European security summit on Monday to map out a future blueprint for peace but Russia's concerns over NATO expansion threatened to dominate the meeting.

Heads of state and government from the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) were expected to agree a final document that will lay out plans for European security in the 21st century, launch a new round of arms control talks and shore up peace in Bosnia.
"Peace demands trust among peoples," Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres told the opening session of the two-day summit.
"We, political leaders, must be the builders of that trust."
Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, standing in for President Boris Yeltsin who is recovering from heart surgery, was due to speak early in the Monday session.
Russia has wasted no time in underscoring Moscow's opposition to NATO plans to take in former members of the now-defunct Warsaw Pact.

Speaking on the eve of the summit, Chernomyrdin repeated the tough line adopted by Russian leaders last week against the Western alliance's eastward expansion, which Moscow says would threaten Russia's security.

"Russia is categorically against NATO expanding eastwards," he told reporters. "There is no need to rush. The fact that Europe is now without blocs is very important. We must work together. We must develop this, strengthen this."
Western diplomats say they would prefer the Lisbon summit, which brings together the United States and Canada with European states, to avoid the debate on NATO enlargement.
The last OSCE summit two years ago in Budapest was wrecked by a row over the same issue and by differences over Bosnia.

The leaders will also hold a series of bilateral meetings on the fringes of the summit -- more than 170 in total. Chernomyrdin was scheduled to meet U.S. Vice President Al Gore, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac.
Representatives from Algeria, Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia, Japan and South Korea are attending the summit as observers, as well as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Russia has little chance of winning support at the summit for its proposals to give the OSCE a more powerful role in European security and act as a counterbalance to NATO.
But by taking a hard line on NATO enlargement, Moscow may win concessions in talks on other issues at the summit, including adapting a 1990 treaty on conventional arms control.

The United States, represented by Gore who arrived on Monday, and most NATO states have indicated they will accept new talks next year on adapting and modernising the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty.

The pact, which commits many of the 54 OSCE states to cut military hardware such as tanks, aircraft and artillery, was concluded during the Cold War East-West divide. Moscow says that, with the breakup of the Soviet Union, NATO forces are superior and a new balance must be worked out.

Officials worked through the night to reach final agreement on the summit documents on issues ranging from ethnic conflicts and human rights to arms control. Diplomats said some issues remained unresolved as the summit opened.

One year after the end of the war in Bosnia, the meeting will agree a continued role for the OSCE there through 1997, working in parallel with the NATO-led peace force, with scope for a further extension through 1998.

Despite concerns over a possible NATO row, some diplomats said they were more worried over hardline positions being taken by Azerbaijan and Armenia over the disputed enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh -- something which could scupper agreement on a final summit document unless it is resolved.
